units.text: REPORTS OF SOCIETIES. The Ureter from the Gynaecologists' Point of View ' Sex Hormones in the Treatment of Breast Cancer ' The Ureter from the Gynaecologist's Point of View

gynaecologists in this country. There are many problems in gynaecology which can only be satisfactorily resolved by close co-operation and consultation between gynaecologist and surgeon and this should occur before operation is undertaken.

The distortion of the ureter and bladder neck which may result from uterine prolapse is well known and in such cases the ureter is very liable to injury at subsequent operations in the region. Ureteric catheterisation has been suggested as a safeguard but may have just the opposite effect. The ureter can always be indentified at the pelvic brim but distally may disappear into dense inflammatory tissue and if definition becomes impossible deliberate division is the procedure of choice. The ureter may be divided unintentionally but if this is recognised no great harm is done. The proximal divided end should be implanted into the bladder, a ureteric catheter being left in situ for 5-7 days. It may at times be necessary to strip the ureter clean from pelvic brim to bladder, and necrosis does not occur if this is done. Much has been written about the importance of preserving the blood supply of the ureter in ^plantation procedures but it would appear that the intramural vascularity is very adequate. Further, after such stripping, ureteric function is preserved.
In certain cases, especially of cancer, interests will best be served by ureterocele anastomosis and gynaecologists should become familiar with this procedure.

It is becoming apparent that certain cases of cancer of the cervix are radio-resistant and that radical surgery should be given a wider application. In such seriously ill patients a one-stage procedure is indicated and this carries a higher risk of complications if uretero-colic anastomosis should prove necessary : too tight suturing pf the ureter into the bowel would appear to have been the cause of fatal uraemia m two cases so treated. In non-malignant conditions, e.g., vesico-vaginal fistula, the original Coffey technique of operating on one ureter at a time is to be preferred. An advantage is that the approach to the left ureter at the second stage can be extra-peritoneal.

There is now the possibility of a new operation described by Mr. Terence Millin to deal with those cases of vesico-vaginal fistula of traumatic origin where there is extensive destruction of the urethra ; the fistula is closed from behind and a new urethra fashioned behind the pubic bone by trocarisation.

The time must come when every case of uterine cancer should be the subject oi consultation between gynaecologist, pathologist, radiotherapist and urologist before treatment is undertaken or refused on the grounds of extension. Discussion : Terence Millin. Uretero-colic anastomosis is a diffcult problem and many results are far from satisfactory. Technique must be improved and consultation between gynaecologists and urologists encouraged. In cases of sloughed ureter after pelvic operations it is essential to wait a minimum of three months before attempting any reparative surgery, as the vascular infected tissues bleed Profusely and will not hold sutures. Deprivation of blood supply plays no part *u the etiology of uretero-vaginal fistula. Sepsis is a definite predisposing factor and the three causative factors are (1) damage at operation, (2) sloughing due to leakage urine not noted at the primary operation, (3) the development of sepsis. Radium ls not-so successful in the treatment of cancer of the cervix as was formerly hoped, ^ud the possibility of damage to the ureters during radical hysterectomy presents a formidable problem and demands better team work between obstetricians, gynaecologists and surgeons. Arthur Jacobs : Simultaneous transplantation of both ureters is preferable in the majority of cases of uretero-colic anastomosis especially as it prevents these very ill or, in benign cases, otherwise healthy women from having j-o undergo abdominal section twice. Furthermore, extra-peritoneal implantation has certain risks : it is well established that fistula due to the ureter coming out of "e bowel is more liable to occur when the extra-peritoneal route is employed.

./ Sex Hormones in the Treatment of Breast Cancer : A. W Kay : Tlie initial report in the Proceedings of the Royal Society of Medicine in 1944 of 168 cases of cancer of the breast treated by stilboestrol therapy showed that in certain cases a very striking response was obtained. These results have since been borne out by other clinical trials, but the results in all series are variable, unpredictable and inconstant.

There is no rationale for this method of treatment. All that can be said is that it may produce beneficial effects and is worthy of trial in the otherwise hopeless case of breast cancer, but in no other.

Good results have been obtained with both oestrogens and androgens. The best response to oestrogens occurs in the older age groups and at all ages the hormone has a marked tonic effect. Pain may be relieved even in cases where there is no other objective improvement. Side effects may be produced of which the most important are breast engorgement, nausea and vomiting, which fortunately usually ceases if therapy is continued, and uterine bleeding which is sometimes associated with enlargement of pre-existing uterine fibroids. Some patients develop resistance to stilboestrol. In all age groups it would appear that androgens have a higher percentage of success. The most successful cases are in the younger age groups.
Larger doses are required, varying from 200-300 ing. testosterone per day. Male side effects, such as voice changes and growth of facial hair are common and may be distressing.

Both androgens and oestrogens promote retention of electrolytes and consequently may give rise to oedema, and congestive cardiac failure may necessitate withdrawal of the drug. Oedema is marked in patients who have had radical mastectomy. Extensive decalcification of bone, especially the spine, may call for supportive measures.

The benefits which may result from hormone therapy are improvement in the patient's general condition and well being, relief of pain, healing of ulcers, resolution of primary and secondary tumour masses. A rise in the alkaline phosphatase level has been cited by Adair as an index of improvement.
There is no precise information about the effect of these hormones on the cancer cell ; in some cases a great increase in fibrous tissue has been demonstrated.

The dosage of stilboestrol is usually 15 mg. daily by mouth, but doses up to 300 mg. have been advocated by Adair. Testosterone is given in doses of 25-300 mg-, commonly 100 mg. intramuscularly three times a week. Methyl testosterone may be given orally.

-_ Treatment should be continued as long as improvement is maintained. If oestrogens fail or cease to be effective androgens should be tried and may prove beneficial. This is not a cure for breast cancer, more than 50 per cent of cases fail to respond.
But the 45 per cent who do respond gain weight, feel better in themselves and may have most gratifying relief of pain and even healing of ulcers and resolution of visible and palpable tumours.

Discussion: A. L. Goodall : In the younger age groups stilboestrol may have disastrous effects in acute cancer of the breast, the patients going rapidly downhill-Many cases have marked reactions to hormone therapy. There is no reasonable physiological basis for this form of treatment. In a series of 160 cases of fibrocystic mastitis who had been treated by oestrogens cancer was demonstrated by biopsy in four.

Oestrogens should not be given in the treatment of chronic mastitis. E. G. Oastler : Is there any direct antagonistic action of these hormones to the cancer cell or is the effect due to overgrowth of the stroma ? A. W. Kay : The fate of the cancer cell is quite unknown. D. F. Cappell : At the present time there is no explanation as to how or why these hormones act as they do in cases of cancer of the breast. Hormones have been claimed to be highly successful in the treatment of leukaemia, but patients so saved from leukaemia have died of cancer. The whole subject is extremely obscure and all we can do is to make observations which may in the course of time lead to some clarification of the problem. The bad effect of oestrogens on fibrocystic disease of the breast is what one would expect knowing what happens in animals. J. Leslie Orr : The general use of hormones by practitioners outside hospitals and without proper supervision is to be deplored. The only justification for the use of hormones is for cases in which well established methods have failed or are inapplicable. In the younger age group a patient presenting with painful breast engorgement should not be given stilboestrol speculatively as the cause may be physiological and miscarriage may result.

The eighth meeting of the session took place in the Faculty Hall, 242 St. Vincent Street, at 8.30 p.m., on 27tli January. Dr. Ian Anderson read a paper on The Diagnosis and Treatment of Simmond's Disease.' Dr. R. S. Patrick delivered an illustrated address on ' Liver Changes in Gastro-Fnteritis.'

The diagnosis and Treatment of Simmond's Disease : Ian Anderson : Few of the hormones produced by the pituitary gland have any biochemical effects directly detectable, and therefore, in the biochemical investigation of Simmond's disease reliance has to be placed on the assessment of the activity of other endocrine glands controlled by the pituitary.

Gonadotropic activity can be assessed by the urinary content of follicle stimulating hormone and the 17-ketosteroids ; thyrotropic activity by the estimation ?f the B.M.R. or by the uptake of radioactive iodine by the thyroid gland. There are three groups of hormones, each with distinctive biochemical effects, produced by the adrenal cortex under the control of the anterior pituitary, (a) androgens, which can be estimated in the urine, (6) hormones controlling salt and water metabolism whose activity can be assessed by the Mayo Clinic water test, which measures the capacity of patients with adrenal insufficiency to produce diuresis when under the influence of a standard dose of water, (c) hormones which influence carbohydrate Metabolism and deficiency of which can be assessed by the insulin sensitivity test.

The clinical picture of Simmond's disease varies, but characteristic features are increasing weakness, loss of libido, anorexia, mental apathy, loss of weight, loss ?f hair, genital atrophy and intolerance of cold. The skin becomes dry and atrophic ; the face presents a striking waxy pallor and the patient looks prematurely old and careworn. Many of these signs may occur in other diseases such as anorexia nervosa a^d Addison's disease and biochemical investigations on the lines suggested can be considerable diagnostic value. The tests used have been the determination of 'he B.M.R. determination of electrolytes, the water tolerance test, the insulin sensitivity test, the determination of the urinary 17-ketosteroids and folliclestimulatory hormones.

The B.M.R. is invariably lowered in Simmond's disease to an extent greater than the clinical condition would suggest. The diagnostic criteria of the water test ?re that in normal persons the maximum urine volume passed in the first four hours 111 the morning after a standard dose of water should exceed the volume of urine Passed in the previous nine hours. In cases of adrenal insufficiency the night urine Volumes were in each case well above the maximum morning volume. In Simmond's disease, where there is both gonadotropic and adrenal cortex insufficiency, the excretion of 17-ketosteroids in the urine sinks almost to zero, less than 2 mg. per hours.

The four essentials in the biochemical diagnosis of Simmond's disease are : ?w B.M.R. ; positive test for adrenal iusufficency ; marked increase in insulin Sensitivity ; virtual absence of 17-ketosteroids from the urine. The ideal treatment ^f?uld be by replacement therapy with anterior pituitary hormone, but the potency commercial extracts is doubtful and the degree of atrophy found in the other endocrine glands as the result of removal of the trophic influence of the pituitary lnakes it unlikely that they would be capable of response to stimulation. Thus rec?urse has to be taken to replacement of the subsidiary hormones. Thyroid ^xtract must be given with D.O.C.A. and adequate salt and water otherwise severe 'uresis with loss of electrolyte may result in a fatal adrenal crisis. The required osage can only be assessed by the patient's response. D.O.C.A. should be given rtially iu a snlall dose, 0.5 nig. intramuscularly daily, the aim being to raise the , -P-. increase vitality and body weight, and thyroid to raise the B.M.R. The ?sage of both should be increased gradually, D.O.C.A. by 0.5 mg. every 4 days st thyroid by 0.5 gr. every 14 days. When the patient appears to be reasonably abilised D.O.C.A. implants?100 mg. for every 0.5 mg.?can be substituted. If le patient shows an incomplete return to normal strength and wellbeing testos-?rone, which promotes nitrogen retention and the building up of body protein, ectrolyte retention, and is essential to relieve anaemia, is given. P}Scussion : Robin Murdoch : It is heartening to see that patients now diagnosed as ttiinond's disease have a much better chance of longevity than was thought Possible when Sheeliau first brought the subject to the fore. Most cases seen in Practice give a history of some difficulty in parturition, post or iutra-partum ?ei)lorrliage but this will not always be forthcoming. It is known that the anterior 11 uitary gland hypertrophies in pregnancy and if by substitution therapy normal genital function can be restored and the patient become pregnant the outlook is extremely good. Two cases of Simmond's disease in the fertile period of life have been so treated and recovered remarkably after pregnancy. A. Slessor : A very useful test of hypopituitarism is the response of the circulating eosinophils to injection of adrenalin which acts on the anterior pituitary causing an outpouring of adrenocorticosterone and of adrenal hormones of the sugar active type which in turn cause reduction of the eosinophils. These cases are initially very sensitive to D.O.C.Aand have a marked tendency to develop subcutaneous oedema. Testosterone in itself has a remarkable salt-retaining effect.
Liver Changes in Gastro-Enteritis : R. S. Patrick : Since May, 1946, close on six hundred cases of acute gastro-enteritis have been admitted to Belvidere Hospital.

The disease is commonest in the very young and very few were over the age of one year and only one of the cases aged more than one year could be described as really ill. In the late summer and autumn of 1947 the disease was very severe and fatal and this coincided with a pneumonia epidemic?in one fatal week half of the patients in the ward died. In 1948 the mortality was 32 per cent and last year 16 per cent, but in a disease whose incidence and severity is subject to such wide variations no significant inference can be drawn from such figures. In post mortem studies ot twenty iatal cases only six showed severe enteritis and this was nio&imarked in the terminal ileum.

The commonest single finding was soft yellow enlargement of the liver due to faity infiltration but this was not seen even microscopically in infants only a few weeks old. Necrosis of the liver occurred in these cases.

Evidences of parenteral infection, particularly purulent otitis media and broncho-pneumonia and skin infections were very common. The cause of the liver changes has excited much speculation and a series of liver biopsies was carried out, 363 biopsies in 160 infants, in an attempt to elucidate the problem. Of these 160 cases 47 died and of these 25 were examined post mortem. In a few cases a slight increase in periportal reticulum has been demonstrated but at a later stage tins has returned to normal and it would seem that in gastro-enteritis fatty infiltration does not persist long enough to produce cirrhosis. Serial biopsies show that while a very severe degree of fatty infiltration may be present at the clinical onset of the disease the disappearance of the fat after clinical recovery is a slower process and takes a week or longer. There is no constant correlation between the severity of the illness and the degree of fatty infiltration, nor does severe fatty infiltration necessarily indicate that recovery will be protracted. While relapses and complications are commonest in cases with severe fatty infiltration they do occur in cases where it is absent. Phospholipids seem to be necessary for the transportation of a proportion of the fatty acids of the body. When they are not available for that purpose fat accumulates in the liver and cannot get to the fat depots in the body. Attempts to supply possibly deficient amino acids, choline and methionine were made, but the results were disappointing : the addition of liver extract and other vitamin i> preparations proved equally unsatisfactory. When intravenous casein hydrolysate was administered, again the response was unsatisfactory and in three of ten cases there was actually a very marked increase in the fatty infiltration. This interference with phospholipide metabolism is not the only means by which fatty infiltration can occur.

There would appear to be a definite relationship between the amount of liver fat and the absence of glycogen from the parenchymal cells. In severe clinical cases there was marked dimunition of glycogen and as soon as there was clinical improvement glycogen returned. It would seem that the fatty infiltration may be due to starvation and if this is so it is more likely to be the result of the primary disease than of underfeeding alone. Iyiver necrosis is rare, quite a different condition; and in two of the three cases in this series from which biopsy material was obtained there was no evidence of preceding fatty infiltrations and no response to intravenous casein hydrolysate. The cause is unknown ; in both types of liver involvement liver function tests yielded negative results and were valueless. Discussion : J. E. Craik : It is interesting to find that, despite extensive fatty infiltration and liver cell damage, the liver function tests yield negative results. As there can, in many cases, be very little functioning liver tissue remaining it ^s difficult to understand why the tests were negative. Recently an adult aged 30 was admitted to the Victoria Infirmary with severe vomiting and diarrhoea, the result of the ingestion of half an ounce of Ferri et Amnion. Cit., as an abortifacient. She died within twenty-four hours and at post mortem the liver was very markedly infiltrated with fat and enlarged. There was no sign of inflammatory reaction and 110 clear reason why she died. J. H. Hutchison : Fatty change is common in the liver in gastroenteritis but bears no relationship to the severity of the illness or to prognosis. It is a result of starvation and does not play any great part in causing death. The findings really stress what still needs stressing, the cause of death in infantile gastro-enteritis is chemical and not pathological. The babies die of a serious upset of electrolyte and acid-base equilibrium and the best way to treat them is to attack that upset by administration of suitable electrolytes. J. B. Rennie : Is it correct to say that the liver parenchyma is necessarily much damaged in fatty infiltration ? In extensive infiltration by carcinoma or leukaemia small areas ?f liver cells continue to function. Eighty per cent of an animal's liver can be removed without causing death. But in infective hepatitis where more liver cells are destroyed or damaged liver function tests do give positive results. T. Anderson : What is most impressive in the sections shown is the extensiveness of liver damage. We have been carrying out work in Knightswood which would suggest that the baby who is bottle fed may be lacking in power to synthesize and break down proteins, and, although one cannot go much further than that, it gives the impression that such babies are in a poorer state of nutrition than are breast fed infants.
